newsitem.title: SERBIA: Authorities shut six Serbian radios, two TVs.
newsitem.headline: Authorities shut six Serbian radios, two TVs.

text.p: Authorities closed down six small private radio stations and two television channels in southern Serbia this weekend, tightening media control ahead of parliamentary and presidential elections later this year.

"Closure of TV Trstenik is a continuation of the plan of the SPS to shut down all free radio and TV stations in Serbia over the next ten days," Democratic spokesman Slobodan Vuksanovic told the independent Belgrade news agency Fonet.
The Trstenik station was shut along with the six radio operations and one television station in the town of Kraljevo.
Media control is vital to the ruling Socialist Party of Serbia (SPS) ahead of the autumn votes.
Vuksanovic said his party would initiate protests throughout Serbia over the crackdown on the free media.
TV Trstenik was the first station which started working independently, not under SPS control, after the victory of the opposition Zajedno coalition at local elections last November.
Freedom of the press figured high on the agenda of the massive Zajedno protests across Serbia which seriously challenged President Slbodan Milosevic's 10-year rule this winter.
Trstenik TV manager Milan Miletic told Fonet the station held all the necessary regular working licences.

Independent B92 radio said inspectors of the federal Telecommunications Ministry began closing six radio stations around Kraljevo in southern Serbia, which carried mostly local news on limited facilities, on Friday and finished on Sunday.
"People in Kraljevo will be able to receive only state media programmes in the future," the radio said.
Police accompanied the teams which confiscated the broadcasters' equipment, the radio said.

The independent newspaper Nasa Borba reported that the inspectors banned all stations in Kraljevo apart from M-radio which has an operating licence and which supports the ruling Socialist Party of Serbia, the paper said.
Kraljevo is ruled by the Serbian opposition but control of the press falls under Socialist-ruled republican jurisdiction. The stations closed were close to the opposition.
The West has repeatedly warned Serbian authorities against cracking down on independent media vital for airing opposition views to the public.
The opposition has accused the state-run Television, the basic disseminator of information to the population too poor to buy newspapers, of being heavily biased in favour of the SPS.
The United States insists the improvement of relations between Washington and Belgrade depends also on improvement of press freedom in Serbia.
Serbian authorities argue that many private broadcasters do not have an operating licence.
